```{r setup}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "#>", fig.align = "center")
options(digits = 3)
```

```{r data}
#| code-summary: "Data and the named birds"
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

data(peng, package = "heplots")    # palmerpenguins, 333 complete cases

col <- c(Adelie = "#F37A00", Chinstrap = "#6A3D9A", Gentoo = "#33a02c")

# the named birds, by row number in heplots::peng
named <- tibble::tribble(
  ~id, ~name,         ~namer,
  283, "Cyrano",       "Thompson",
  124, "The BFG",      "Thompson",
  304, "Tinkerbell",   "Thompson",
  166, "Average Joe",  "Thompson",
   10, "Socrates?",    "Friendly",
   35, "Falstaff?",    "Friendly"
)

peng <- peng |>
  mutate(id         = row_number(),
         bill_shape = log(bill_length) - log(bill_depth),
         stoutness  = log(body_mass) / 3 - log(flipper_length)) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  mutate(z_shape = c(scale(bill_shape)),
         z_stout = c(scale(stoutness))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(named, by = "id") |>
  mutate(label = ifelse(is.na(name), NA, paste0(name, " (", id, ")")))
birds <- filter(peng, !is.na(name))
```

## Overheard at Biscoe Point

<!--
MF's idea: open with a conversation among penguins, as a block quote. Rough draft from
penguin-names.md, to be worked up. Keep it short: three or four exchanges, then pivot to
"they have a point".
-->

> "Hey Bro, have you noticed? All these scientists measured us up the wazoo, published papers, and now our
> data is famous, used to teach statistics and data graphics all over the world. And they don't even know
> our names, even with those tags on our flippers."
>
> "And why didn't they bother to give us the Big Five personality scales? Those orange Adelies are often
> narcissistic extroverts, not very open to experience."

They have a point. The [Palmer penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/) are
identified only by numbers: their row numbers in a data frame. Even those aren't stable. They
depend on whether the few birds with missing measurements were dropped: Cyrano, whom you'll meet
shortly, is number 294 in `palmerpenguins::penguins` and number 283 in `heplots::peng`. This post
is an attempt to right this injustice to the 344 birds on Biscoe, Dream and Torgersen islands near
Palmer Station who allowed themselves to be measured for science from 2007 to 2009.

<!--
Pivot: a few of them do have names. Name them here, briefly, as a teaser:
Cyrano and Hook Nose (from my book), the BFG, Tinkerbell and Average Joe (from Cara Thompson).
The question of the post: what makes each of them unusual, and do the names fit?
-->

A few of them do have names. Cara Thompson named four: Cyrano, the BFG, Tinkerbell and
Average Joe. I borrowed Cyrano for my book, and added a Hook Nose of my own. So the questions for this
post are: what makes each of these birds unusual, and do their names fit?

## Naming names

I first got to know the Palmer penguins when I found that they made good examples for methods of
multivariate data visualization. I adopted them as a running example in my book,
[_Visualizing Multivariate Data and Models in R_](https://friendly.github.io/Vis-MLM-book/), where
they turn up in nearly every chapter.

### Three noteworthy birds

In [Chapter 4](https://friendly.github.io/Vis-MLM-book/04-multivariate_plots.html), I went looking
for multivariate outliers. As in the Bob Marley song, I found "three little birds, at my doorstep."

The main tool is the squared Mahalanobis distance, $D^2$, of each bird from the
centroid of all four measures (bill length and depth, flipper length, body mass), taking their
variances and correlations into account. Three birds came out on top: cases 283, 10 and 35. A
chi-square QQ plot showed that only one of them, 283, is a true outlier. The other two are just the
most unusual of an ordinary lot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cqplot
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "70%"
#| fig-cap: "Chi-square QQ plot of the penguins' squared Mahalanobis distances on the four measures, with a 95% confidence envelope. Only case 283 lies outside it."
library(heplots)
vars <- c("bill_length", "bill_depth", "flipper_length", "body_mass")
DSQ <- Mahalanobis(peng[, vars])

cqplot(peng[, vars],
       id.n = 3,
       col = col[peng$species],
       pch = c(19, 17, 15)[peng$species],
       ref.col = "grey",
       what = "Penguin numeric variables",
       cex.lab = 1.25)
```

Plotting bill length against bill depth with those three labeled, two of them looked odd for their
species. Case 283, a [Chinstrap]{.chinstrap}, has a remarkably long bill, so I called her "Cyrano",
after the long-nosed hero of Edmond Rostand's play. Case 10, an [Adelie]{.adelie} with a short, deep
bill, became "Hook Nose". Case 35 looked unremarkable in that view and stayed nameless.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bill-noteworthy
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "80%"
#| fig-cap: "Bill length against bill depth, with 95% data ellipses and regression lines for each species. The three birds with the largest $D^2$ are labeled."
three <- order(DSQ, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
peng_plot <- peng |> mutate(note = id %in% three)

ggplot(peng_plot,
       aes(x = bill_length, y = bill_depth,
           colour = species, shape = species, fill = species)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = note), show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(1.5, 4)) +
  geom_text(data = subset(peng_plot, note),
            aes(label = id), fontface = "bold",
            nudge_y = .4, colour = "black", size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x,
              se = FALSE, linewidth = 2) +
  stat_ellipse(geom = "polygon", level = 0.95, alpha = 0.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.85, 0.15))
```

The names stuck, at least for me. Cyrano reappears throughout the book: dancing around the edges of a
grand tour, at the extreme ends of a biplot, as the most influential case in a multivariate linear
model, and finally getting a weight of zero in a robust fit. "Bye-bye Cyrano---it's been fun---but we
can get along nicely without you." That is the point of a name: a reader can follow Cyrano from chapter
to chapter in a way they can't follow "case 283".

### Where "Cyrano" came from

I thought I had made up the name. It turns out I hadn't. I'd seen it in
[Cara Thompson](https://www.cararthompson.com/)'s poster for useR! 2022,
[*Level Up Your Labels: Tips and Tricks for Annotating Plots*](https://www.cararthompson.com/talks/user2022/),
filed it away, and forgotten where it came from. My code for the book still had a comment,
`# From Cara Thompson`, above her lines that picked out the birds (with her name misspelled, which
didn't help).

Her poster is a lesson in annotation. Its plot, titled *"Perfectly proportional penguins---with a
few exceptions!"*, shows flipper length against bill length, and replaces a legend and a lot of
explanation with a few well-placed text boxes. Four birds get names and a sentence each:

* **The BFG**: "Sitting comfortably within the cluster of Gentoos, this Adelie penguin defies the
  predictions of his species on both flipper length and bill length."
* **Tinkerbell**: "The smallest penguin in the set defies the odds on weight for her species and
  flipper and bill length."
* **Average Joes**: "The Gentoos tend to stick to their trend, with very few outliers. Heavier
  penguins have longer flippers and longer bills."
* **Cyrano**: "With an exceptionally long bill and the shortest flippers bar one among the
  Chinstraps, this little guy is sure to stand out!"

![Cara Thompson's plot from her useR! 2022 poster, [*Level Up Your Labels*](https://www.cararthompson.com/talks/user2022/). © Cara Thompson, reused under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).](images/thompson-annotated-penguins.png){#fig-thompson}

She picked these birds by eye, from one plot. As we'll see, every one of her descriptions holds up,
except perhaps "little guy": Cyrano is a female.

### Who gets a label?

Thompson's poster had a second effect on me. In her plot, and in mine in the book, the labeled
birds were chosen by hand, and the labels were added by a small piece of `ggplot2` plumbing: compute
something, make a logical variable for the cases to label, then add a `geom_text()` layer for just
those rows. It works, but you have to do it again for every plot.

Base R graphics handle this better than `ggplot2`, thanks to the `car` package. Nearly every plotting
function in `car` takes an argument like `id = list(n = 3, method = "mahal")`, and labels the 3
points furthest from the centroid, with no further work. The `method` can be `"x"`, `"y"`, `"r"` for
residuals, or a vector such as Cook's distances. Labeling unusual points becomes a decision about
*which criterion*, not a chore.

I pulled that selection logic out into a function,
[`heplots::noteworthy()`](https://friendly.github.io/heplots/reference/noteworthy.html), which takes
`x`, `y`, `n` and a `method`, and returns the row numbers of the points to label. The criterion
needn't come from the two variables on the axes. Here it finds the book's three birds, using $D^2$ on
all four measures, for a plot of just two:

```{r noteworthy}
#| code-fold: show
noteworthy(peng$bill_length, peng$flipper_length, n = 3, method = DSQ)
```

That isn't what Thompson would have found with a formula. The default, `method = "mahal"`, on the
two variables in her plot picks out a different set:

```{r noteworthy-2d}
#| code-fold: show
noteworthy(peng$bill_length, peng$flipper_length, n = 6, method = "mahal")
```

Cyrano (283) is first again, but the rest (179, 314, 272, ...) are birds on the edges of the overall
cloud, which spans three species. None of the BFG, Tinkerbell or Average Joe is on that list. Her eye
was doing something the formula wasn't: judging each bird *against its own species*. I'll come back to
that.

The next step was to make this a `ggplot2` layer, `stat_noteworthy()`, so that any plot could say
which points to label in the same vocabulary. With help from the
[ggplot2 extenders club](https://github.com/ggplot2-extenders/ggplot-extension-club/discussions/91),
I got a working version. Getting it *generally* right turned out to be harder:

<!-- MF: check/expand. From heplots/dev/noteworthy/ggextenders-noteworthy.md -->

* **With groups**, should it pick the $n$ most unusual points overall, or $n$ in each group? The
  usual `ggplot2` habit is per group. A statistician usually wants the most unusual points in the
  plot as a whole. Both are reasonable, so it should probably be an option.
* **With facets**, the selection should be done separately in each panel.
* **Higher dimensions**: the penguins' case is the hardest. The criterion ($D^2$ over four variables)
  lives in more dimensions than the plot shows. A `ggplot2` stat sees only the variables mapped to
  aesthetics, so there's no clean way to hand it the others.

So `stat_noteworthy()` is still in the development folder of `heplots`, a branch partly leafed out,
waiting for another season. Meanwhile the penguins wait for their names.

## One view in 2D

<!--
Thompson's view, with all six birds. Point: her four were picked by eye from this one plot,
and every one of her labels checks out. But Socrates and Falstaff look ordinary here: what makes
them unusual can't be seen in bill length and flipper length.
The BFG "sits comfortably within the cluster of Gentoos": a discriminant analysis on these two
variables calls him a Gentoo (p = 0.97), but not on all four, where his deep bill gives him away.
-->

```{r}
#| label: fig-thompson-view
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Thompson's view of the penguins: flipper length against bill length, with point size showing body mass. Her four named birds are joined by two more from my book."
ggplot(peng, aes(bill_length, flipper_length, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = body_mass), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = birds, aes(size = body_mass), shape = 21,
             colour = "black", stroke = 1.1) +
  geom_label_repel(data = birds, aes(label = label),
                   size = 4, fontface = "bold", fill = alpha("white", 0.85),
                   box.padding = 0.6, min.segment.length = 0, seed = 2022,
                   show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 4, breaks = c(3000, 4500, 6000),
                  labels = \(x) paste(x / 1000, "kg")) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Flipper length (mm)",
       colour = "Species", size = "Body mass") +
  guides(size = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = "grey50")),
         colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.02, 0.98),
        legend.justification = c(0, 1), legend.box = "horizontal",
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey80"))
```

## What makes a penguin unusual?

<!--
Recap of the two earlier posts in two short paragraphs, with links: bill size and shape
(log L ± log D), body size and stoutness (log F ± log M/3). Within species these are nearly
uncorrelated (except bill size with body size, r = 0.70), so a bird's oddity can be traced
to one or two of them.
"Unusual" means relative to its own species: z-scores within species. Explain why: a Gentoo
bill on an Adelie is news; a Gentoo bill on a Gentoo isn't. Contrast with the book's D²,
which ignores species: the BFG ranks 89th that way, 3rd within species.
-->

```{r}
#| label: tbl-birds
#| tbl-cap: "The named birds, as z-scores within their species on bill shape and stoutness."
birds |>
  select(name, id, species, sex, bill_length, bill_depth, flipper_length, body_mass,
         z_shape, z_stout) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(z_shape) + abs(z_stout))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
               col.names = c("Name", "Case", "Species", "Sex", "Bill length", "Bill depth",
                             "Flipper", "Mass", "z shape", "z stoutness"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-shape-stoutness
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 7.5
#| fig-cap: "Bill shape against stoutness, as z-scores within species. The ellipses hold 68% and 95% of all birds. Each named bird is extreme in a different direction."
lim <- c(-4.2, 4.2)
ggplot(peng, aes(z_shape, z_stout, colour = species)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = 1), level = 0.95, colour = "grey40",
               linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = 1), level = 0.68, colour = "grey40",
               linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = birds, shape = 21, size = 3.5, colour = "black",
             aes(fill = species), stroke = 1.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_label_repel(data = birds, aes(label = label),
                   size = 4, fontface = "bold", fill = alpha("white", 0.85),
                   box.padding = 0.7, min.segment.length = 0, seed = 2022,
                   show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col) +
  coord_equal(xlim = lim, ylim = lim) +
  labs(x = "← stubby    Bill shape, log(length / depth)    slender →",
       y = "← lean    Stoutness, log(mass^(1/3) / flipper)    stout →",
       colour = "Species") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.88, 0.14),
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey80"))
```

## A rogues' gallery

<!--
One short paragraph per bird, in the order of the figure, going around the compass.
Each: what the data say, then whether the name fits. Use the species CSS classes:
[Chinstrap]{.chinstrap}, [Adelie]{.adelie}, [Gentoo]{.gentoo}.
Facts are in penguin-names.md, "Reading it" and "Reading her labels against the data".
-->

### Cyrano (283): the long nose

<!-- Chinstrap female. L/D 3.26, above every other Chinstrap (next 2.93) and above the Gentoo means:
a Gentoo's bill on a Chinstrap's body. Also stout (short flippers, tied 2nd shortest among Chinstraps).
Thompson's label is exact. The name fits; the footnote about her being female ("Roxane"). -->

### Hook Nose, or Socrates? (10): the snub nose

<!-- Adelie male. The lowest raw L/D of all 333 (1.64). Bill short (4th percentile) and deep (97th).
"Hook Nose" was my mistake: depth measures thickness at the base, not curvature; nothing in the data
measures a hook. Socrates: the famous snub nose (Plato, Xenophon). The opposite of Cyrano.
Caveat: within species, a Gentoo male (183) is stubbier still. Another unnamed bird. -->

### Falstaff? (35): the stout one

<!-- Adelie male. Ordinary bill. Stoutest bird of all 333 (M/F³ 0.75; next 0.69): 4650 g on 184 mm flippers.
The book's Ch 5 guessed "much heavier than most, with short flippers", from a biplot of the smallest
dimensions. Nameless until now. -->

### Tinkerbell (304): the slight one

<!-- Chinstrap female. Lightest of all 333 (2700 g; next 2850), on ordinary flippers and bill length:
the least stout bird in the data. The mirror image of Falstaff. Thompson's name fits. -->

### The BFG (124): the impostor

<!-- Adelie male. Longest flippers of any Adelie (210 mm); long bill. Looks like a Gentoo in 2D.
Within species, the 3rd most unusual bird (after Cyrano and Socrates), though the book's D² missed him (89th).
Slender bill, lean body. "The BFG": big, long-limbed, gentle. -->

### Average Joe (166): the control

<!-- Gentoo male. Flipper length exactly the Gentoo male mean; within-species D² ranks 319 of 333.
Thompson used him for the Gentoo trend. Every study needs one. -->

## What's in a name?

<!--
Wrap-up.
- The two families of names: Thompson's from children's fiction and Rostand (Dahl, Barrie);
  mine continue the literary theme. The pairs: long nose and snub nose; stoutest and slightest.
- The statistical point, in one paragraph: names help us remember points; good variables tell us
  *why* a point is unusual. A 2D view of the raw measures picked out some birds and missed others.
- Invite readers to name 183, or propose better names (Pug? Puffin?).
- Back to the penguins: "Now they have names. The personality scales will have to wait."
